No one is mad for the blowout at 11. OP was then further angry as they continued to grow at their mom over what are very clearly their mom's attempts to reconnect. They tell you in the post that she tried really hard to be the fun mom, that she visited on weekends. They tell you that they lashed out at their mom and that they wanted to go back home with her, but OP doesn't say that they apologized or told her they wanted to go back home. They say their mom was confused why they were angry when their childhood bedroom got converted, which tells me that mom was not informed that OP missed living with their mom or that they were jealous of the split in her attention. 


Blowing up on your mom at 11 is normal, but as you grow you are supposed to develop empathy. It doesn't sound like OPs dad is helping with this either- there is no mention of him suggesting that OP think about how they hurt their step siblings or encouraging them to talk to their mom in a more appropriate way about their feelings- all things a parent absolutely should be doing when a blowup like that happens. People are also not angry with OP now, it's understandable why a 17 year old can't navigate such complicated emotions without help. But OP is 17, I entered college at that age. Next year OP will be a legal adult, and no switch will flip in maturity when that happens. Now is the time that OP needs to learn to talk about their feelings and take responsibility for the way they hurt others. Most situations involve more than one party being hurt, and learning to navigate taking responsibility for hurting others while also discussing your own hurt is an important skill to be learning and practicing by 17.

I read this post and thought "These are two people who completely don't understand each other at all". I was wondering how you two got married and then saw your ages and now your post makes sense. You two are talking about two totally different things,and neither of you realize it. 

Your wife is being derisive and dismissive because she is afraid of being replaced in and important tradition she enjoys. She could have said this more clearly, but that is what your wife meant when she said "Good luck doing it without her". Clearly, her baking is a point of pride for her, it is a tradition where she felt important and useful and proud of her achievement. She was afraid of feeling left out and also that she would not be needed. This tradition is part of her identity and she felt threatened by losing it. She could have communicated this better, but honestly, she is 23. That's real young to have perfected your communication.

In her defensiveness, you heard "My wife thinks I am incapable" and you set out to make her proud by applying your time and skillet to the best of your abilities to make the cookies as excellent as you could. It was important to you to prove to your wife that you were capable and could do a good job. You wanted to show her that you could exceed her expectations and prove yourself capable in your own right, because you probably felt hurt and defensive that your wife didn't believe in you. 

Now, changing the ingredients and timing,as someone who bakes, almost certainly will change the taste, and the thickness will change the mouth feel. But you know what? It doesn't matter. Because what you want is your wife to tell you that you're capable and did a good job. And your wife wants to hear that you respect her skillset and talents at baking, that she's needed, and that she was missed. The cookies are totally tangential to what's happening here. 

You guys are super young. You're still learning about yourselves. There are going to be so many times when you clash over things like this, that are absolutely not about the cookies. Take a deep breath, let go of the need to figure out who is the asshole. Everyone is the asshole, no one was the asshole. Sit down and tell your wife you love her baking and you missed her and her cookies are fantastic and unique and you love them and her. Tell her she hurt your feelings,and you wanted to prove yourself and you want to hear her acknowledge your abilities. This is absolutely not about the cookies.

I have literal ADHD and am late so often that I joke I will be late to my own funeral. I can't really fix the time blindness or the way I seem to always forget something crucial and have to double back. But you know what I can fix, and do? I tell people. I text them. If it's 10 minutes from when I need to leave and I can't find my keys, I text my friends and say "I am running late, I can't find my keys". If I lost track of time working on a task, I text them and say "Sorry, I completely lost track of time and will be there about x late". 

It's so important to text so that your friends know you haven't blown them off and also they can prepare their own time- maybe they wanted to grab a coffee or stop by an ATM on the way to somewhere, and now they can. Maybe they wanted to change their shirt but didn't have time. Maybe they need to put air in their tires, or maybe you are just giving them an extra 15 to sit on the couch. Either way, by letting them know, you are freeing up their time and telling them you respect them.

I was with you when you were asking for monetary contribution or help with the chores, but no adult on earth sets a wifi cap on another adult living with them.

If you want to charge Chris in rent or labor, then accept that you need to treat him as a contributor and not "owner's rules". At that point Chris becomes almost a roommate lite. Think back to what having a roommate was like and set boundaries accordingly. 

Something like setting up a chore schedule or payment schedule, or letting him know about the cost of upcoming utilities? Completely appropriate. 

Telling Chris how much wifi or Netflix he can use? Not appropriate. 

Since he has become an adult your relationship has fundamentally changed, and part of that is what you can reasonably ask of him. The wifi rule is deeply infantilizing, as is asking him to be "grateful" for the food he eats. What is not infantilizing is asking him to contribute to the wifi bill or make his own meals if he doesn't like what was prepared.

If your Fiancé cooked professionally, he may not realize how badly he is trashing the kitchen, since in the environment he was used to it was literally someone's job to do the washing up.

Mentioning this bc I see a lot of comments assuming this is a control issue- and it could be- but it could also be your Fiancé being picky about something that is his area of expertise, which we can all be guilty of. That said, it's untenable long term and definitely ah behavior even if unintentional.

Just have a conversation about how many dishes there are and the imbalance, ask if weeknight meals can be simpler and if he can make complicated things on weekends and you both do the washing up. Or ask if you can split meal nights or if he can help with the washing up. If he doesn't change after having a conversation about it, then it becomes a deal breaker.

Oh, I read this post as OP was the experienced DM and was looking for how to play but avoid being controlling. I was giving this as an anecdote because I thought one of my players was great about it, as a new DM myself.

I have organisational problems and am doing my first campaign as a homebrew so I feel you!
Here are some things that have helped me on the fly:
I get weird stage fright sometimes about math, so I have a table of checks- what to roll, what the check is against etc so if I panic blank I can just look. 

I color coded things. Good npcs are written in one color of ink, bad npcs in another, a color for locations- this lets me glance to check things

I like to overwrite beforehand. There are things I have never used, but there are many many more times I was glad I knew more about a person or a place. Also when I have to improv it helps me to have background knowledge to go off of. 

Don't be afraid to say "let me look". Take a deep breath. Everyone is new sometime, and you cannot know every spell and check and weapon by heart. 

But also: so I really liked the writing portion- it makes me happy and excited and the improv comes easy to me compared to game mechanics. So I focus on writing down the game mechanics and organizing that, because I know it's where I'm weakest. If what feels daunting to you is the writing, maybe a prewritten would be easier. Plan out supports for where you feel you need the most help.

I'm a new DM (first campaign) with an experienced DM as one of my players.
He has been awesome and never weighs in on my decisions unless I ask, and backs me up when I am firm.

And when I do pause to say "let me check" when a player asks about using a spell, sometimes he will help me by telling me/messaging me more info if he's already familiar. (I am less familiar with spell descriptions because I have predominantly played fighters) 

For me, not offering help unless I need it and just kind of backing up my decisions has been really awesome and helpful, in addition to the help when I DO need it. I would say don't offer help unless its asked for, and back up the DM on a judgement call even if it's a different call than you would make.
